items.title: The End of Stephen Miller’s Recusals
items.description: S tephen Miller spent his first weekend as White House chief of staff on the patio at Mar-a-Lago, huddling with President Trump and Natalie Harp, his executive assistant, about how to approach the next two years with the House and Senate under Democratic control. Katie Miller—the podcaster, political consultant, and wife of Stephen—spent the weekend in the Washington area, rearranging her own life. “I make every decision based on what’s best for my children and our family,” she wrote yesterday on X, before announcing that she had decided to wind down her podcast. But that was not all that was changing. For months, Stephen Miller has recused himself from matters of policy that involve Katie Miller’s other financial interests at the direction of the White House counsel. That meant that Stephen did not work on issues involving the media company Paramount, where his wife had been seeking a podcast deal, or anything to do with space policy or artificial intelligence, because his wife, a longtime adviser to Elon Musk, also worked for SpaceX, the owner of the Grok artificial-intelligence assistant. All of that changed today. Katie Miller severed her employment with SpaceX, sold her stock in the company, and forfeited her right to future equity that had not yet vested under her contract, according to a person familiar with the moves. Over the weekend, she also ended a separate contract with Paramount for a planned podcast deal. As a result, a White House official told me this afternoon, “Stephen Miller is no longer subject to any recusals and may fully participate in all meetings and policy matters.” Katie declined to comment. White House lawyers had previously ruled that Katie Miller’s podcast advertising sponsorships from companies seeking official favor from her husband did not require recusals, because sponsorships carry a different ethical significance than consulting arrangements. Sugar-soda boosters at the American Beverage Association, the utility Southern Company, and the Merchants Payments Coalition, a group pushing for legislation to reduce credit-card swipe fees, had all purchased time on her show. But now even those potential conflicts will not be an issue, after a couple more already-recorded episodes from her podcast are released. “Nothing is more important than raising our four kids,” she wrote. “While I’ve loved the podcast, the time commitment is too great and now is the time to step away.” [ Read: A chief of staff who ‘will crack skulls’ ] The Millers met during the first Trump term, when both were working for the administration. Katie Miller later worked as a press secretary and communications director for Vice President Pence, before becoming an adviser to Musk, the founder of SpaceX and CEO of Tesla. During the transition following the 2024 presidential election, Katie Miller worked as an adviser to future Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., before joining the White House as a special government employee who advised Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency. When she left the White House, she maintained her consulting work for Musk and SpaceX, leading the White House counsel to advise that Stephen Miller recuse himself on related issues. When Katie Miller began working closely with Paramount, offering to help arrange a company party for Trump before the White House Correspondents’ Dinner, Stephen Miller expanded his recusals to cover related issues. Katie Miller’s career change comes amid a public uproar over possible improper influence in the White House, after the former adviser Calley Means went on Joe Rogan’s podcast to allege “demonic” efforts to influence White House policy by lobbyists with close ties to senior officials. Concern about corruption , often focused on the president’s own for-profit efforts in office and the business deals of his children, became a significant issue in the recent midterm elections. Gallup found in September that 89 percent of U.S. adults believed that corruption was widespread in the government, a proportion that had risen 10 points in just one year to the highest level in the two decades that the polling question had been asked. After Trump announced his new chief of staff on Friday afternoon, Katie Miller responded on X: “Watching your best friend and spouse achieve their dreams is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.” She kept the commentary going through the weekend. When Politico published an article about how she had lobbied for the promotion, Miller responded: “BREAKING: Wife supports husband. If your wife doesn’t do this, find a new one.”

items.title: The Inconvenient Truth at the Center of the Immigration Debate
items.description: Have liberals learned anything from the border crisis that helped return Donald Trump to office two years ago? Many have not, if a recent report from the American Civil Liberties Union is any indication. The group claims to offer a “way forward” for the country’s asylum system, which has become a back door for economic migrants. But the ACLU instead recycles arguments that immigration advocates have made for decades. Too many progressives fail to understand, or acknowledge, the real reason migrants, including those intending to seek asylum, cross the border illegally: People come when they think they can stay. I have been working on border and immigration policy for more than 20 years, serving in senior roles at the White House and the Department of Homeland Security as well as Senate staff. I have seen, up close, surges in illegal immigration under both Democratic and Republican presidents. Again and again, the loudest and most extreme voices have set the immigration agenda for each party, to the detriment of the country. Despite Trump’s concession in yesterday’s 60 Minutes interview that his administration’s handling of immigration was “too tough,” his elevation of the anti-immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff suggests that this trend will continue. Immigration advocates who deplore the Trump administration’s aggressive tactics have an obligation to propose realistic, constructive alternatives. Yet on the left, the ACLU and other immigration advocates continue to argue that enforcement at the border, including restrictions on asylum eligibility, do not prevent or deter illegal immigration; they simply create pent-up demand and encourage migrants to attempt more dangerous routes. As a result, according to advocacy groups, the only way to stem the tide of illegal immigration is to address the underlying problems that push people to leave their countries, and to provide more legal pathways for these migrants to come to the United States. [ From the November 2026 issue: The babies left behind in America ] In reality, the United States’ inability to promptly remove those who lack a legal basis to remain in the country has been the driving force behind every major surge in illegal immigration since the Obama administration. The U.S. asylum system , created by Congress at the height of the Cold War, presumes that almost everyone who passes an initial screening deserves legal protection. As a result, more than 80 percent of people who claimed asylum at the border from 2014 to 2019 were released into the country, yet immigration judges ultimately granted asylum in less than a fifth of these cases. This legal process can take years, during which seekers are allowed to apply to work, which makes it easy for economic migrants to game the system. Nobody would spend $15,000 in smuggling fees and experience the mortal dangers of the journey north if they didn’t believe that they could stay and get a job. Before 2011, only about 2 percent of people who crossed the border illegally claimed asylum. But as word got out that most people who claim asylum at the border are let in, the percentage of undocumented border crossers who claimed asylum steadily increased , to 16 percent in 2013 and then to 59 percent in 2023––far outstripping the U.S. government’s capacity to process applications in a timely manner. The Obama administration experienced its first surge in migration from Central American families claiming asylum at the border . At the time, advocacy groups persuaded senior officials and key members of Congress to focus on the root causes of illegal immigration—such as violence, corruption, and political instability in other countries—instead of tackling the incentives in the asylum system that encouraged migrants to come here. In 2016, the U.S. invested a record $750 million in aid in projects to create jobs, enhance governance, and improve security in the region. The initiative made modest improvements , but could not fix the problems that were encouraging so many people to flee. What kept illegal border crossings at manageable levels on President Obama’s watch was an increase in border security, a more stringent enforcement of immigration laws within the country, and record-high deportation numbers—for which immigration advocates gave the president the not-so-flattering title of “ Deporter-in-Chief .” At the start of Trump’s first term, the new president’s tough talk about the “invasion” at the border seemed to have deterred some would-be migrants and so further reduced illegal crossings. But migrants soon realized that they could still game America’s asylum system. By 2019 Border Patrol apprehensions along the southwest border exceeded 850,000 , up 115 percent from 2018. Trump’s initial response—to separate the families of asylum seekers at the border—was both ineffective at deterring migration and abhorrent to many Americans. Other restrictions on asylum that his administration introduced in 2019, such as the “Remain in Mexico” program that required asylum seekers to wait in Mexico as their cases played out in U.S. court, had inhumane consequences but did curb border crossings. Emergency measures during the coronavirus pandemic cut the number of crossings even more. But as the pandemic eased, people began moving north again. When President Biden took office in January 2021, illegal crossings had already begun to surge, averaging 70,000 a month from October 2020 through his inauguration. Instead of addressing this problem, Biden spent his first days in office fulfilling campaign promises to immigration advocates. He announced a moratorium on deportations and ended Trump’s asylum restrictions, sending a clear message that the U.S. border was going to be open. He also put Vice President Harris in charge of a strategy to invest more than $5.2 billion in private-sector funds to create more economic opportunities in Central America, which once again did not reduce immigration from the region. Another common argument among immigration advocates is that expanding access to legal immigration will take pressure off the border. The problem is that no realistic amount of legal pathways will satisfy global demand to immigrate to the United States. When I was in the Biden administration, we oversaw the largest expansion of lawful pathways for migrants in a generation, explicitly to reduce illegal immigration from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela. What we found was that illegal crossings dropped only when they triggered clear consequences at the border, such as repatriation of ineligible asylum seekers to Mexico. The United States can and should increase legal pathways for immigrants, but the goal should be to enhance economic growth and reunite families—not to prevent illegal immigration. There is a cruel irony in the fact that, by pushing policies that enable economic migrants to gain entry into the United States via the asylum system, human-rights advocates have encouraged migrants to put their lives at risk on their way to the U.S. border. In 2023, I was part of a delegation to Colombia and Panama to urge those governments to close the Darién Gap —a treacherous and sometimes lethal route between the two countries through which migrants trekked to the United States. From a helicopter, I saw thousands of people streaming out of the jungle after a week-long ordeal. On the ground, we met children who survived the journey but were alarmingly weak from exhaustion and dehydration. We learned that human-rights groups were providing migrants with supplies—including birth control for women, many of whom would be sexually assaulted by smugglers during the illegal crossing. I believe that none of those migrants would have risked these dangers if they didn’t think that the United States would let them stay. [ Read: The problem with shutting down ICE in blue states ] The Biden administration learned the hard way that the only reliable way to deter illegal immigration was to restrict asylum —such as by setting more stringent screening criteria and requiring asylum seekers to set up interview appointments in advance and use a designated port of entry—and increase resources to enforce these laws at the border. In 2023, these curbs on asylum-seeking worked initially, but encounters at the border with Mexico surged when enforcement by Mexican authorities waned, and fell sharply when this enforcement expanded in concert with U.S. efforts in early 2024. By mid-2024, when Biden introduced more asylum restrictions at the border, encounters dropped by roughly 55 percent—from about 120,000 in May to about 56,000 in July. But by then, the perception that his party couldn’t or wouldn’t keep the border under control had helped doom Democrats’ prospects in the November election. Following the advice of immigration advocates when he took office and waiting too long to change course were among Biden’s biggest mistakes. At least some progressive leaders seem keen to avoid these mistakes. “I think we’ve learned the lesson,” Michigan Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed said about the chaos at the border under Biden in a preelection 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat. “You can humanely enforce the border.” Voters are plainly tired of the wild swings in policy between permissiveness and cruelty. The Trump administration’s poll numbers on immigration suggest that the president’s merciless approach to migrants—which led to the fatal shootings of people protesting enforcement actions—contributed to his party’s stunning electoral defeat last week. Trump promised a crackdown on the “worst of the worst.” Instead, his administration has redeployed federal resources that were once used to address and prevent more serious crimes, such as terrorism , fentanyl smuggling, and child sex trafficking, to deport otherwise law-abiding people in the United States. The Trump administration has also waged an all-out war on legal immigration, rescinding the lawful status of about 1.8 million immigrants , restricting access to green cards, halting visa processing in mostly nonwhite countries, and cutting naturalizations of new U.S. citizens by 75 percent. This despite the warnings of economists that these policies would measurably harm economic growth . American agricultural producers now say that ICE’s indiscriminate raids are hurting domestic farmers and threaten to raise grocery prices even further . Like Biden, Trump is listening too closely to the most radical voices in his coalition—and he has paid a political price for it. Every single congressional district on the U.S. border with Mexico is projected to be held by a Democrat next year. But his promotion of Miller, the architect of his cruel and nativist approach to immigration, suggests that he has not learned from this electoral rebuke. Most Americans hold heterodox views on border and immigration policies: They want strong enforcement at the border, but they want this enforcement to be fair and humane, and for people who have otherwise lawfully contributed to their communities for years to be able to stay. Immigration policy shouldn’t be just the province of ACLU-style progressives and hard-liners such as Miller. Lawmakers should stop pandering to the extremes of their bases and step up to fix America’s broken immigration and asylum system once and for all.

items.title: Semaine du numérique : la 21e édition prévue, du 24 au 27 novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou
items.description: Le secrétaire général du ministère de la Transition digitale, des Postes et des Communications électroniques, Borlli Michel Jonas Somé, a animé une conférence de presse, lundi 9 novembre 2026, à Ouagadougou. Il a, à l’occasion, annoncé la tenue de la 21e édition de la Semaine du numérique et du Salon International des TIC et de la Bureautique de Ouagadougou (SITICO), du 24 au 27 novembre 2026, dans la capitale. La Semaine du numérique va vivre sa 21e édition, du 24 au 27 novembre 2026, à Ouagadougou, conjointement avec le Salon international des technologies de l’information et de la communication et de la bureautique de Ouaga-dougou (SITICO) qui l’accompagne. C’est l’annonce faite, à la presse, par le secrétaire général (SG) du ministère de la Transition digitale, des Postes et des Communications électroniques, Borlli Michel Jonas Somé, lundi 9 novembre 2026, dans la capitale. Selon lui, les deux évènements vont se dérouler sur le site du Salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO) autour du thème : « Souveraineté technologique : accélérer la transformation digitale sécurisée et inclusive ». Par ailleurs Président du comité national d’organisation (PCO), il a indiqué que la maîtrise des infrastructures, des données, des technologies et des compétences numériques constitue un levier stratégique pour renforcer l’indépendance, la résilience et la compétitivité du Burkina Faso. « Cette 21e édition réunira les administrations publiques, les entreprises, les professionnels du numérique, chercheurs, les établissements d’enseignement, les startups, les partenaires et le grand public », a dit le PCO. Pour lui, plusieurs activités permettront d’aborder les enjeux techniques, de présenter des solutions et de rapprocher les innovations des besoins réels. Il s’agit, a-t-il précisé, des « Conf’days » qui vont être le principal espace de réflexion et de partage d’expériences, de village des startups et de l’innovation, « le voyage vers le futur invitera les visiteurs à découvrir, à travers les différents scénarios ce que pourrait être le Burkina Faso de 2030, des démonstrations de robots humanoïdes et quadrupèdes et la formation vont constitués une autre attraction », a ajouté le PCO. La Nuit des lauréats au menu Le SG du ministère en charge de la transition digitale a, en outre, souligné que la Nuit des lauréats, prévu vendredi 27 novembre 2026, va consacrer les talents et les acteurs qui se distinguent par leur contribution au développement du numérique. Concrètement, quel rôle joue le SITICO ? Face à cette question, Borlli Michel Jonas Somé a expliqué que le SITICO constitue l’une des composantes majeures de la Semaine du numérique. « Le SITICO constitue une plateforme de rencontre entre les entreprises, les fournisseurs de solutions technologiques, les opérateurs, les institutions financières, les startups et les utilisateurs », a-t-il fait savoir. Le PCO a aussi soutenu que le SITICO sera une tribune pour les entreprises de présenter leurs produits et services et les professionnels de découvrir les technologies disponibles. Le SITICO, a-t-il ajouté, sera également l’occasion pour les organisations de rechercher des solutions adaptées à leurs besoins et aux visiteurs de mieux connaître les possibilités qu’offrent les outils numériques. Il a informé que le salon sera organisé sous forme de galerie marchande, avec des espaces d’exposition repartis par catégorie de stands Diamond, Gold, Silver et bronze. Borlli Michel Jonas Somé a fait comprendre que de nombreux stands seront disponibles au prix de 250 000 FCFA, 200 000 FCFA et 150 000 FCFA. Il a fait savoir que le site www.semainedunumerique.bf est accessible à toutes les personnes ayant besoin d’informations complémentaires. Il a lancé une invite à la population à venir découvrir les solutions numériques, comprendre leurs usages et mieux apprécier les possibilités offertes au quotidien. La semaine du numérique instituée en 2003 sous l’appellation de Semaine nationale de l’Internet, puis consacrée Semaine du numérique en 2019, constitue aujour-d’hui le rendez-vous national de référence pour la promotion, la vulgarisation et l’appropriation des technologies numériques au Burkina Faso. Boukary BONKOUNGOU Rasmatou OUEDRAOGO (Stagiaire)

items.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 17 people
items.description: At least 17 people have died, and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey. All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, one of the country’s leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air. The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below. Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labour Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan originally said the death toll was 16, but the Health Minister, Kemal Memişoğlu, later announced that one of those who had been critically injured had later died, taking the toll to 17. Eyewitnesses at the scene said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck. In a statement, the company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant’s electric arc furnaces. Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told the media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble. Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued. At least five people have been arrested, according to BBC News’s Turkish service, citing local media reports. The Habas plant is in Aliaga district of Izmir, a major port and one of Turkey’s main shipbreaking hubs.

items.title: Ukraine-Russie: ce que l'on sait sur la reprise des négociations
items.description: Des négociations entre l'Ukraine et la Russie, sous médiation américaine, doivent avoir lieu mardi et mercredi à Abou Dhabi, après plus de huit mois d'interruption du fait de la guerre au Moyen Orient. Voici ce que l'on sait sur ces pourparlers qui visent à trouver une issue diplomatique au conflit – le plus meurtrier en Europe depuis 1945 – déclenché par l'invasion russe à grande échelle de l'Ukraine en 2022. L'Ukraine sous pression Sur le plan diplomatique, l'Ukraine, en proie à des bombardements russes constants et meurtriers, est sous pression. La Russie pilonne à nouveau, depuis plus d'un mois, son réseau énergétique, faisant craindre un nouvel hiver sans chauffage, eau courante et électricité pour des millions d'Ukrainiens. Parallèlement, cet automne, le président américain Donald Trump s'est fortement rapproché de Moscou: il a vilipendé son homologue ukrainien Volodymyr Zelensky et conclu un accord avec le Kremlin pour la livraison de diesel russe, malgré les sanctions occidentales toujours en vigueur, suscitant la consternation de Kiev. Les Ukrainiens sont « très pessimistes » quant aux initiatives de l’administration Trump, et « contraints » de s'adapter à « la stratégie américaine », dit à l’AFP l’analyste Volodymyr Fessenko. Un récent cessez-le-feu dans la région de Kherson, à l'initiative de la Première dame américaine Melania Trump, a permis des évacuations humanitaires et a été respecté par les deux camps. Un « précédent très positif », selon M. Fessenko, qui pense que Kiev va chercher la « désescalade » par « le biais de telles trêves locales ». Jusqu'à présent, Moscou a refusé un cessez-le-feu prolongé sur tout le front. La délégation ukrainienne sera dirigée par le négociateur Roustem Oumerov et incluera également Kyrylo Boudanov, le chef de l'administration présidentielle ukrainienne et ex-dirigeant du renseignement militaire. Le président russe Vladimir Poutine refuse de rencontrer directement Volodymyr Zelensky pour négocier, hormis à Moscou. Sur le front, ses troupes sont empêtrées dans une guerre d'usure où l'omniprésence des drones bloquent tout mouvement d'ampleur. Elles grignotent encore du terrain dans certains secteurs, mais au prix de très lourdes pertes. Ces derniers mois, une contre-offensive ukrainienne a même permis à Kiev de reprendre du terrain et soulager la pression autour de Kramatorsk et Sloviansk, les grands bastions de la région de Donetsk, dans l'Est, qui échappent toujours au Kremlin. Poutine a fait de la prise de la région de Donetsk son objectif principal, mais, à ce rythme, elle pourrait mettre des mois, voire des années. Kiev refuse de se retirer de cette région très défendue, estimant notamment que cela permettrait au Kremlin d'attaquer ensuite davantage son territoire, en l'absence de garanties de sécurité solides. Lors des négociations à Abou Dhabi, la délégation russe sera à nouveau dirigée par l'historien nationaliste Vladimir Medinski, et incluera également un vice-ministre des Affaires étrangères, Sergueï Riabkov. « Il s'agit d'une équipe très sérieuse, capable d'aborder un large éventail de questions : sur le plan militaire, le règlement des enjeux territoriaux et les garanties de sécurité (…) mais aussi la sécurité européenne », a dit à l'AFP Alexandre Gabouev, directeur du Centre Carnegie Russie-Eurasie. Trump veut un « très grand accord » Mises en suspens en raison de la guerre en Iran déclenchée par des bombardements israélo-américains, ces négociations sous la médiation des États-Unis reprennent après les visites en septembre, à Kiev et à Moscou, des émissaires américains Jared Kushner et Steve Witkoff. Après avoir rencontré la semaine dernière l'émissaire russe Kirill Dmitriev — présent à la Maison Blanche en même temps que des responsables ukrainiens — Donald Trump a prédit un « très grand accord » avec la Russie sur l'Ukraine qui pourrait « englober toute l'Europe ». Jared Kushner a, lui, déclaré que les États-Unis travaillaient sur un accord visant à établir une « architecture de sécurité européenne plus large ». MM. Kushner et Witkoff ont été accusés de faire preuve de complaisance envers la Russie. Et des médias américains ont rapporté que les Américains chercheraient à conclure, en coulisses, des accords commerciaux d'envergure avec Moscou. Le rôle des Européens Depuis le retour de Donald Trump à la Maison Blanche, les Européens craignent que Moscou et Washington ne concluent un accord sans les consulter. Lundi, M. Zelensky a dit s'être « coordonné » avec l'UE avant les pourparlers. « L'UE, l'Otan, l'E3 (France, Allemagne et Grande-Bretagne) seront présents, en marge de ces discussions tripartites », a indiqué lundi un responsable de l'UE ayant requis l'anonymat. Ecartant toute participation directe des Européens, le Kremlin a souligné lundi que les discussions seraient strictement trilatérales. La Russie a cherché à écarter l'Europe des discussions et la plupart des dirigeants européens n'ont eu que peu, voire aucun contact avec Vladimir Poutine depuis 2022. Le mois dernier, le président finlandais Alexander Stubb et le Premier ministre norvégien Jonas Gahr Støre ont néanmoins eu un échange téléphonique, fait rare, avec M. Poutine, qualifiant ces discussions de « substantielles ». The post Ukraine-Russie: ce que l'on sait sur la reprise des négociations appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Coopération Burkina-Chine: une délégation chinoise découvre le patrimoine historique et artisanal burkinabè
items.description: Dans le cadre de leur séjour au Burkina Faso, une délégation chinoise a effectué, le lundi 9 novembre 2026, une visite au Mémorial Thomas-Sankara et au Village artisanal de Ouagadougou. Cette immersion leur a permis de découvrir deux facettes importantes de l’identité nationale : l’histoire du pays et la richesse de son patrimoine artisanal. Au Mémorial Thomas-Sankara, les visiteurs ont approfondi leurs connaissances sur l’histoire du Burkina Faso, notamment sur l’héritage du père de la Révolution d’août 1983, son engagement patriotique ainsi que les idéaux de souve-raineté et de solidarité qu’il a portés. A l’issue de cette étape, les membres de la délégation ont exprimé leur admiration pour l’esprit de solidarité du peuple burkinabè, qu’ils considèrent comme une force essentielle pour relever les défis du développement. La délégation a également salué le leadership du Président du Faso, le camarade capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, qu’elle associe à la poursuite des idéaux de Thomas Sankara, à travers la Révolution progressiste populaire (RPP). La visite s’est poursuivie au Village artisanal de Ouagadougou, où la délégation a pu apprécier la diversité des créations et la richesse du savoir-faire des artisans burkinabè. Cette découverte a mis en lumière le potentiel du secteur artisanal national, notamment en matière de valorisation des produits locaux. DCRP/MICA

items.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss’s affair with alleged Chinese spy
items.description: Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the boss of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy. The US President said he spoke with chief executive Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. “I asked him that question, ‘Did you have any idea she was a spy?’ He said ‘I had no idea she was a spy’ and I really believe him,” Trump told reporters. China has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”. Nvidia, who has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company’s secrets or national security were compromised. But later on Monday, Trump said the FBI was now looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

items.title: À Mayotte, l'interminable attente des demandeurs d'asile congolais [1/2]
items.description: L'attente et l'incertitude : c'est ce que vivent les migrants congolais arrivés à Mayotte. Après avoir fui la guerre dans l'est de la RDC, ils demandent l'asile à la France. Mais sur le territoire, aucune structure n'est adaptée pour les prendre en charge. Les délais avant d'obtenir la protection internationale sont extrêmement longs. Sans pouvoir prétendre aux droits associés, ils sont 1 800 à vivre dans le camp informel de Tsoundzou, dans la plus grande précarité.

items.title: Farouk Aliu Mahama confirms 2028 Yendi parliamentary bid
items.description: Former Member of Parliament for Yendi, Dr Farouk Aliu Mahama, has confirmed his intention to contest the constituency’s parliamentary seat in the 2028 general election on the ticket of the New Patriotic Party (NPP). His decision follows what his supporters describe as weeks of appeals from youth groups, traditional leaders, elders and other community stakeholders urging him to return to active parliamentary politics. The former MP says his decision is driven by a desire to continue his development agenda for the constituency, which he has described as the “Great Yendi Dream”. The declaration comes ahead of the NPP’s November 10, 2026 deadline for prospective parliamentary aspirants to formally register their interest through the party’s online portal. A vision interrupted Dr Mahama represented Yendi in Parliament from 2021 to 2025, having won the constituency in the December 2020 general election. During his tenure, he facilitated a number of development initiatives, which his supporters say included road improvements in farming communities, the construction and renovation of educational facilities, vocational training opportunities for young people and interventions to support farmers. These initiatives, according to his supporters, formed part of his broader vision of transforming Yendi into a modern and economically vibrant constituency, which they have branded the “Great Yendi Dream”. However, his parliamentary tenure ended following his defeat in the December 2024 general election. Some of his supporters have attributed the defeat to internal divisions within the NPP, although that explanation remains their assessment of the factors behind the electoral outcome. Says commitment to Yendi remains Despite losing the parliamentary seat, Dr Mahama’s supporters say he has maintained his engagement with constituents through educational assistance, community interventions and other forms of support. Among the recent interventions attributed to him is the donation of a 100KVA generator to a community in the constituency reportedly affected by unreliable electricity supply. He is also said to have supported a young Yendi indigene pursuing medical studies abroad. Explaining his decision to contest again, Dr Mahama said: “I did not leave Yendi. Yendi never left me. I am back to finish what we started together – the Great Yendi Dream.” His supporters have welcomed the announcement, describing it as a response to calls for his return to represent the constituency. One social media user, commenting on the development, praised the former MP for maintaining contact with constituents after leaving Parliament. “When he lost, other politicians disappeared. FAM stayed. He paid our fees, he came to our events, he fixed our light. That is why we called him back. We want our MP back,” the user wrote. Supporters call it ‘The Great Return’ Supporters of Dr Mahama have christened his proposed comeback “The Great Return” , presenting it as an opportunity to revive what they consider an unfinished development agenda for Yendi. They say his return would also provide an opportunity to address divisions within the party and consolidate the development initiatives they credit him with facilitating during his four years in Parliament. His confirmation sets the stage for another contest for the Yendi parliamentary seat, subject to his participation in and success at the NPP’s parliamentary primaries.

items.title: Beyond the fanfare: Why Ghana’s tourism economy deserves serious investment
items.description: Ghana possesses an economic advantage that many countries would spend fortunes attempting to manufacture: an internationally recognised cultural identity, remarkable historical assets and a growing tourism market. What remains is the opportunity to organise these strengths into a larger, more competitive industry capable of attracting investment, creating employment and generating sustainable national wealth. The numbers provide a compelling starting point. According to the Ghana Tourism Authority’s 2025 performance figures, international arrivals reached approximately 1.31 million. Visits to tourist attractions increased by seven per cent to 1.79 million, while licensed tourism enterprises expanded by 6.1 per cent to 7,109. Travel trade businesses recorded 18.6 per cent growth, with food, beverage and entertainment enterprises expanding by 8.2 per cent. Estimated international tourism receipts stood at US$4.34 billion. These figures establish a substantial market with opportunities across hospitality, transport, entertainment, cultural production and supporting services. The visitor experience indicators are equally encouraging. Reported satisfaction reached 99 per cent for Ghanaian friendliness and 98 per cent for airport facilities and formalities. More than 60 per cent of international visitors were repeat travellers. Business travel accounted for approximately 31 per cent of international arrivals, while the entertainment and conference segment expanded by 14.3 per cent. Taken together, these indicators suggest an industry capable of supporting a broader range of commercially viable investments. They also explain why Ghana’s tourism development agenda deserves attention from financial institutions, development partners and private investors. During IMANI Africa’s Centre for Policy and Education working visit to the Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts, our delegation, comprising IMANI President Franklin Cudjoe, Vice President Selorm Branttie, and associates Princess Umul Hatiyya Ibrahim Mahama and Kay Codjoe, examined opportunities for strengthening the sector’s economic contribution. Our engagement revealed a policy direction centred on connecting tourism, cultural heritage, creative industries, infrastructure and private enterprise. This integrated approach creates opportunities that extend beyond conventional destination promotion. Tourism generates demand across multiple industries. Hotels purchase food, furniture and professional services. Conferences require transport, accommodation, catering and technical support. Cultural attractions create markets for guides, manufacturers, designers and entertainment businesses. The economic potential becomes considerably greater when these activities are connected through deliberate investment and commercially sustainable partnerships. Cultural production presents another opportunity. Ghana’s textiles, traditional craftsmanship, historical narratives and creative industries possess commercial value that can support manufacturing, exports and intellectual property development. The Ministry’s attention to cultural merchandise, trademarks and creative ownership provides a basis for strengthening these markets. Appropriate legal protections, credible certification systems and improved access to distribution networks could help Ghanaian producers compete internationally while preserving the interests of traditional custodians. During our engagement, IMANI also explored augmented reality, digital heritage interpretation and historically authenticated storytelling as opportunities for Ghanaian historians, filmmakers, animators and technology enterprises. These technologies could improve visitor experiences while creating new commercial products and professional opportunities. The approximately US$4.5 million Korea-Ghana heritage cooperation programme, scheduled for 2026 to 2030 and covering six coastal heritage sites, provides an opportunity to connect conservation with improved destination management. Such initiatives demonstrate the range of investment opportunities emerging at the intersection of tourism, technology and cultural preservation. Financing is another important component. The 2026 Budget allocated GH¢20 million each to the Creative Arts Fund and Film Fund, with initial releases of GH¢5 million towards each subsequently reported. These commitments provide a foundation for supporting creative enterprises, although their development impact will depend on effective implementation and measurable beneficiary outcomes. Development finance institutions, commercial banks and private investors could complement public resources through appropriately structured financing for commercially viable projects. The opportunity is to develop an investment ecosystem in which public policy provides direction, private capital supports enterprise expansion and communities participate meaningfully in economic returns. IMANI sees value in a comprehensive Ministry performance report covering January 2025 onwards, documenting sector achievements, investment partnerships and development outcomes. A proposed Reset Tourism Conference could similarly connect government institutions, traditional authorities, investors and creative enterprises around practical investment opportunities. Both initiatives could strengthen coordination, transparency and investor confidence. The Ministry’s integrated policy direction provides a framework for developing these opportunities. The sector’s recorded growth offers a credible basis for further engagement, although individual investment decisions will require feasibility assessments, reliable financial information and appropriate safeguards. Ghana’s tourism economy should increasingly be evaluated through enterprise development, employment, investment, visitor expenditure, heritage conservation and the participation of local communities. The potential benefits extend well beyond tourism operators. Agriculture, manufacturing, transport, technology and professional services all stand to participate in a more commercially developed tourism sector. For investors and development partners, the proposition deserves examination on its economic merits. Ghana has an established visitor market, expanding formal business activity, valuable cultural assets and opportunities for investment across several connected industries. The next phase requires sustained financing, institutional cooperation and commercially disciplined implementation. Ghana’s tourism sector has demonstrated measurable growth. With appropriately structured investment and sustained policy coordination, that growth can support a broader and more productive national economy. The opportunity is substantial, and the case for serious investment deserves to be heard. By Kay Codjoe | IMANI Africa

items.title: La policía de Paraguay descubre una bóveda blindada con tecnología israelí en la mansión del expresidente Santiago Peña
items.description: Los agentes fiscales que el domingo por la tarde se dispusieron a allanar la lujosa mansión veraniega del expresidente paraguayo Santiago Peña en San Bernardino —a unos 45 kilómetros de Asunción— tenían el dato de un informante sobre una bóveda secreta oculta tras las paredes. No la hallaron de inmediato. Tras una minuciosa búsqueda, detectaron la puerta disimulada y, tras vencer varios obstáculos, lograron ingresar a una habitación de pánico. Allí tropezaron con un segundo blindaje de acero equipado con claves digitales, llaves físicas y lectores biométricos de huella dactilar e iris. Esta vez no hubo manera de franquear el acceso. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Trump questions midterm elections integrity after previously accepting results
items.description: US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, days after saying he would accept the outcome. “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday. This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results. Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week’s elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free. Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called. In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voor explaining what he meant or without providing specific evidence of what this referred to and whether he believed there had been error or wrongdoing. Vote-count reporting on election night proceeded as normal, according to Charles Stewart III, a political scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). “We saw across the nation the standard patterns we see in terms of when the votes are reported,” he said. Stewart also reported that Florida and Georgia, some initial results came in quickly because they already have the results of early and mail ballots. Trump has previously tried to cast doubt on the integrity of elections he lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms. “We would have won easily if I was on the ballot,” Trump told CBS News, the BBC’s US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House. Surveys ahead of the election from several pollsters and news outlets suggested that Republicans could lose seats in both the House and Senate. As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats in the midterms, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress even as counting continues in some races, like in Alaska and Mississippi. “State laws and practicalities are such that some states will just take longer to count,” said Ruth Greenwood, director of the Election Law Clinic at Harvard Law School. “That doesn’t mean anything nefarious is occurring—we just need to trust local election officials to count every vote and tell us the results when they are done.” The outcome has been clear since election night. Trump told the New York Times then: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with [Democrats]”, adding: “We’ll probably work something out.” He has also offered his own analysis of why Republicans lost, acknowledging on Fox News that the Iran war had contributed to the defeat. “People agree with what I’m doing on Iran but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline – I understand that,” he said. Vice-President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war, which began in February and which has severely disrupted global oil and gas supplies – causing costs to soar, as the reason their party lost the election. In the run-up to the midterms, Trump made claims about widespread voting fraud, despite evidence that it is rare. He and his allies alleged for months that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden, had been rigged against him. His lawyers and allies spent weeks trying to litigate the results, but courts repeatedly struck down their challenges. The justice department during his administration has made unprecedented attempts to exert more federal control over elections – a power the Constitution primarily delegates to individual states. Days before these midterms, it filed controversial lawsuits in federal courts challenging the count and certification of votes in states like California anvote counts but judges ruled aem in nearly all instances. Election law experts, state officiaitand local elections offices told the BBC they had spent months preparing for a scenario in which the White House or election sceptics questioned the votes’ legitimacy. Despite the intense focus around election integrity on both sides of the debate, top state and local election officials have reported a mostly smooth process so far for the 2026 midterms. Extreme weather did force some location closures, and a handful of reported administrative or technical issues slowed the process in some local jurisdictions.

items.title: Congress vs. Hegseth
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Back in February, when the United States and Israel first attacked Iran, President Trump said that it would be a “short-term excursion.” Now, eight months later, as the war with Iran remains without conclusion, the president and his party are dealing with its consequences. As Vice President Vance put it last Tuesday, when Republicans were ousted from their seats in the House and the Senate—not to mention governor’s mansions and statehouses—in a fierce rebuke to the administration’s policies: “The reason we lost is the war.” If voters swung Congress to Democrats in response to the war and its effects, what comes next? Democrats have said that they will vote to end the war; they’ve said, with some Republican support, that they will begin impeachment hearings for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. But after naming the hard-line adviser Stephen Miller, the architect and champion of some of the president’s most aggressive domestic and foreign policies, as his chief of staff, Trump may as well double-down on the agenda he’s chased for the past two years. This week on Radio Atlantic , our staff writers Nancy Youssef and Tom Nichols discuss where the administration goes from here, what options exist to get out of Iran, what to make of Hegseth’s potential impeachment, and how the Defense Secretary has changed the relationship between American democracy and the American military. The following is a transcript of the episode: Nancy Youssef: The most enduring impact [Pete] Hegseth has had, in addition to the war, is on personnel. These are people with 20, 30 years experience, and then there’s all the impacts you don’t see—the captains and the majors who are looking at what’s happened to those ahead of them and saying, I’m not gonna stick around . That’s years and years of investment that has been lost, and will take years and years and years to replace. Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic . I’m Adam Harris, and today, we need to talk about the war in Iran. Voters cared about the war in this election. An AP poll showed that seven in 10 registered voters wanted to see it end. After Democrats rode a blue wave back to power last Tuesday, Vice President J. D. Vance wrote on social media, “The reason we lost is the war.” Now Democrats are exploring the legislative tools they have to act as a check on the administration: They have the War Powers Act, they could withhold military funds through appropriations. But as hard-line adviser Stephen Miller takes over as the new White House chief of staff and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth continues to enthusiastically defend his position and the war, the question remains: Where does the administration go from here in a war of their own making? Joining me to discuss are my colleagues Nancy Youssef and Tom Nichols. Let’s get to questions. Harris: Tom, welcome back to the show. Tom Nichols: Thanks, Adam. Harris: Nancy, great to see you. Nancy Youssef: Great to be with you. Harris: Nancy, right after the election, we saw Republicans across the spectrum jump to blaming Iran and the Iran war for their loss. Vice President J. D. Vance quickly tried to distance himself from the conflict, and then Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released a video in support of the war, saying: Pete Hegseth: Peace through strength is once again American military policy. Our commander in chief demands it, and so we deliver it. Harris: What does his reaction tell us about the discord within the administration? Youssef: Well, Pete Hegseth was the most vocal advocate of this war, not only internally within the administration, but publicly as well, arguing that this was a just fight, that the United States was stopping Iran from having a nuclear weapon—all without releasing key details about what precisely was happening on the ground or at what cost it was coming to the United States in terms of munitions. And so I think the five-minute video was as much about Iran as it was about threats of an impeachment hearing that Tom Massie put forth before the last session, and Speaker [Mike] Johnson notably relieved Congress so that they wouldn’t have that hearing. There’s at least six charges, some of them related to the war as well as to the boat strikes and some of the other actions that the secretary’s taken. Hegseth: A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly. Youssef: And so in a weird way, the secretary’s sort of conceding that he faced impeachment by putting out this video and saying that the military needed to come to defense and fight the fight. He didn’t say exactly against whom, but there you go. But he launched a very forceful defense for an impeachment that hasn’t happened yet. But I think more than anybody, he is personally tied to this war because of his advocacy for it. I think if you’re a legislator thinking about impeachment, that video also signaled what he will do if impeached, which is to try to use it as a form of leverage with the president and potentially for his future political career and say that he’s being targeted much in the same way that [Donald] Trump has felt that he got targeted with some of the previous impeachments against him. And so the question becomes, I think, if you’re in Congress, is this the best way to do it, and is this the best time to do it, particularly if the impeachment itself might not lead to a conviction in the Senate? Harris: Tom, we’re seeing this post-midterms shakeup. Stephen Miller is the new chief of staff. Pete Hegseth is under fire from Congress. What does the last week mean for what we can expect out of the White House after the midterms? Nichols: Well, for one thing, the president’s already set the tone: It wasn’t my fault. Had I been on the ballot— which he was, in a way —we would’ve won these things. And so, there’s gonna be a lot of blame-storming going on. Harris: I guess I should say too: What does it mean for the war in Iran? What does it mean for the White House strategy in the war with Iran? Nichols: Well, for the war in Iran, that’s really hard to say because, in theory, Miller has told the president that they have to get out. But that requires Donald Trump admitting a mistake, giving a W to the regime in Tehran, because it will survive and just washing his hands of it. So I suspect that, at least in the short term, it’s gonna be more of what we’re seeing now, that the president acts as if the war is pretty much over. In his interview with Ross Douthat, he said when Ross asked him, What about the strait being closed? And he said, But it’s open . To which, you know, yes, it’s open because there are U.S. Navy ships right now staying there at great expense and a certain amount of risk. And I suspect that you’ll have this kind of phony war going on, where it’s neither peace nor war but it’s to get it out of the public eye and somehow be able to claim what Trump has always wanted to claim. Since the first few weeks of the war, when regime change didn’t happen, what Trump’s really wanted is: Give me a way to say that I won so that I can get out of this thing . And of course that wasn’t helped—I mean, to bring it back to Pete Hegseth—it didn’t help that Pete Hegseth, at least until May, was going out there and saying: We’re killing it. We’re winning. We’re going gangbusters . Important to note that it’s been now six months since the Defense Department has bothered to give a press briefing. And I think that’s what to expect from the war. That there will be stories about a strike here or there, kind of the way maybe—and it’s an imperfect analogy—but kind of the way that the second Iraq war kind of trailed off. You’d open the paper and say, Oh, we struck some targets in northern Iraq , or, Our planes were fired on as they flew over southern Iraq . But I think that will suit the Iranians just fine. The president again was asked what is in the future, and he said, All those countries are gonna pay every penny that we’ve spent on this war . That’s not going to happen. So, who knows? Harris: You mentioned the interview with Ross where he’s like, Well, the ships are passing through the strait. The strait is open. And he says it’s at great expense, and he’s like, Well, it’s not at great expense . Nancy, can you talk about the expense to this point of the war and what’s necessary in order to keep it over there, as it were? Youssef: So the expense is that naval blockade, which is a very heavy military effort. It takes a number of ships. There are two aircraft-carrier groups in the region right now. There is talk of a third one joining in the coming weeks, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, which is currently near Singapore. When you have that many ships in the region, it means you cannot have naval assets in Europe, in Asia, in the area that Stephen Miller’s particularly interested in, the Western Hemisphere. There just aren’t enough assets to have that kind of lift in the strait and do missions in other places. Moreover, it comes at great risk to not only the ships that are there because the Iranians are targeting them, but ground forces in the region as well, and we’ve seen that happen. And so we’ve seen an extra supplement of air defenses in the region and at the expense again of other parts in the region. We see this, for example, in the inability of the United States to provide further munitions to Ukraine. The U.S. simply doesn’t have it. And remember, the Iranians are firing cheaply made drones and in some cases even ballistic missiles against the United States. It’s much more expensive, much more costly, much longer to resupply air defense capabilities like the THAAD and the Patriot. So that’s sort of the immediate cost. But I think Tom’s point is an important one, in terms of where we are in the war. I think right now we’re seeing sort of three options, in terms of what the president is trying to do. We heard him yesterday say that it was highly unlikely that the U.S. would go back to war, and I think he’s saying that for one of three reasons. Either it’s a head fake and the United States is gonna resume strikes. Or he thinks it’s part of a negotiation tactic. Or he’s just saying it. But whatever it is, he has signaled he does not want to go back. The big change, though, for the Iranians, is twofold: One, Iran thinks that they have leverage in this conflict and don’t need to make any capitulations. And two, that midterm election has bolstered their confidence and their ability to negotiate. And so while the president may try to kind of punt making this decision, at some point, both the cost of the blockade to the U.S. military and the Iranians’ unwillingness to hold this position or to stick to it will make that position untenable. There is a clock ticking in all this. And so while the president wants to keep it in the distance, at some point—I can’t tell you when or how—that will not be a sustainable position. Harris: When we’re back, how the Democratic wins in the midterms might affect the path of the war. [ Break ] Harris: Nancy, Democrats now have an opportunity to do what they said they wanted to do: rein in the war. What are you all hearing now from Democrats, now that they’ve won the election, about possibilities for reining in the war? Youssef: So I think a couple things. One is the impeachment hearing, because if you have an impeached secretary of defense, that certainly—even if he’s not convicted—that certainly puts a spotlight on the war itself. Because even if it’s not the only reason, it’s one of several reasons, and it requires a reexamination. I think the second thing you’re hearing is questions about funding for the Pentagon. One of the problems that the Pentagon’s facing now is: It’s running out of funding. Hegseth is asking for $1.5 trillion, and we’ve heard bipartisan concern about that level of spending without getting any transparency, in terms of what’s happening in terms of the war. Harris: How abnormal is that level of spending, $1.5 trillion? Youssef: We’ve never had that. So usually, defense spending, if you were to make a chart, it kinda goes up and down. So World War II spikes, then it goes back down. Then it goes back up again for Korea, then goes back down. Then it goes up for Vietnam, then it goes back down. And then after 9/11, it just steadily increased. And so what we’ve seen is a growing and growing defense budget. What’s interesting is that they’re talking about increasing defense spending while reducing the number of troops in Europe; while reducing the number of troops in the Middle East, potentially; while sort of focusing on this hemisphere, and yet asking for a larger defense budget. So it’s not just the number, but it’s incongruent with what they’re saying they want to use the Pentagon for. And so they’re running low on funds as it is, and I think Hegseth might be a form of leverage that they try to use to say: If you want us to continue to approve funding, we need to see a change at the top . The other thing I think you’re gonna see a push for is a lot more access to information that legislators and the public used to have about the conduct of war. We don’t know with any fidelity what the stockpile situation is in terms of munitions, what damage happened to the bases, how much it’ll cost to fix, which bases will be fixed, what that means for the future of U.S. military posture. How do you continue to have naval forces in the Middle East when you’ve lost the basing access you need to restock those ships and have liberty visits for the troops? Very basic questions haven’t been answered. And I think one of the things you’ll see, if nothing else, is a push for more of that. Now, whether they get it is something else because there’s been a real tension between the Hill and the secretary. But those answers, I think, are necessary to understand and really hold the department accountable for its conduct of the war. You can’t do it if you don’t have basic facts about what it’s done so far and at what cost. Harris: Earlier this month, Military.com released a poll saying that 53 percent of active service members say they want to separate from the military sooner because the military is becoming more politicized. This is a lot. Tom, how is the administration affecting this decline in morale among service members? Nichols: From the first day of his first term, Donald Trump has attacked the traditions of American civil-military relations. All presidents have done—you know, when they show up at military academies or they go to a military base ostensibly for a nonpartisan event—all presidents skate that line every now and then because they like to have the military as kind of a backdrop to what they’re doing. Donald Trump has left that line in the dirt miles behind him. He has tried actively to tell the military: You are a constituency of the Republican Party and of my support group personally. You are part of me, rather than America . And that hurts morale. I taught for 25 years at the Navy War College, and I taught hundreds of officers. And they all have very—you know, these are men and women of strong political opinions. Have a drink at the O Club, the Officers’ Club, you’ll hear them. But in a way, they took great pride in what I always called the “miracle” of American civil-military relations, which is that we are the most powerful military in the world, and yet no threat to our democracy whatsoever. I think people don’t realize how amazing that is: that a massively powerful military that is absolutely contained within the democratic structure of a large and vibrant and diverse country. And I think that, for many of them, the military is a refuge from politics; that when they go to work and they fly a helicopter or, they’re leading PT, whatever they’re doing, it’s not political. They’re one organization, one mission. And Donald Trump has really divided them about that. And when you start introducing that suspicion—about promotions, about people kind of getting the side eye because of something you might have said—that turns us into a Soviet military, not an American military. That turns us into a Third World military. And that serves Donald Trump’s purposes just fine because, again, he wants the military to be actively engaged in politics. I wrote a piece a while back where I was sort of desperately yelling for somebody to do something about Trump going to Fort Bragg and saying, Come on, let’s all talk about how much Joe Biden sucked . And I said, “Where’s the Army chief of staff? Where’s Randy George?” And of course, Randy George probably—I never spoke to General George about it, but he was soon to be fired. And I think that’s the other problem with morale, is that all of these men and women are looking up the chain and saying, All the day that I do things —I was never in the military; this is something I learned from observing and talking with officers over a quarter of a century—that they look up the chain and they say, Whatever happens in politics, we have this very stable community, this very stable chain of command. People are promoted; they retire; they come up the ranks . When Pete Hegseth inserts himself into those processes and says, All you people on this promotion list, you’re fine except for you, you, you, and you , and those four people are Black, female, disfavored groups in Hegseth’s eyes, because he thinks they were DEI hires, people start to wonder: How stable is that chain of command? What’s happening here? And so it doesn’t surprise me at all that a lot of people would say, You know what? If I’m going to be living in a very politicized, messed-up situation where people are promoted because of politics or demoted because of how they look, I could do that and not have to wear uncomfortable boots every day . And I think that’s really unfortunate. I think the damage to the civil-military relationship in America is a lot deeper than—we’ll realize in a few years just how much Pete Hegseth has damaged the institution of the United States military. Youssef: You know, it’s funny: The question you were asking about the politicization of the military, it actually ties to the Iran war as well, because when you tell people that your promotion is contingent on your loyalty, politically, or your loyalty to the president or the perception [of] that, what it leads to is people less willing to give their best military advice, which they are supposed to do. They’re not supposed to just salute and follow orders, whatever they are. They are supposed to bring forth their best military advice, and I think you saw that in the run-up to the decision to launch these strikes on Iran. So many people had been fired or demoted or pushed out—an unprecedented number—that the lesson people took was not to give their advice, but to salute even when they thought maybe the decision was less than ideal, because to do otherwise risked their jobs, and they’d seen their predecessors leave before them. Moreover, the people who came in afterwards often had less experience than those before them because the system was not designed for this many people to be fired in this way. And so younger and younger people were coming up the chain. The only thing I want to add—and I think it’s an important thing to note—U.S. service members do not take a personal pledge to a person or a president. They take an oath to defend the Constitution, and that is by design because we as a nation have decided we don’t want militaries loyal to any person. That has been a basic foundational principle of the United States military that begins all the way to the oath. And the more we’ve deviated from that—in many ways, the Iran war offers an example of the perils of that—that you get a military that offers different advice than it would, if it believed that it was protected. And so back to your original question: what does Congress do? I’m curious if the Congress, both lame-duck and afterwards, starts to back some of these officers more. I think what’s been striking to me is we’ve seen so many people fired, demoted, pushed out, and, really, almost silenced from the Hill about it. Even though these guys are signed off by the Hill, we haven’t heard anything. Are there going to be hearings in which some of these fired generals and admirals are called back? Is there going to be a public discussion about the impact of this? Because the most enduring impact Hegseth has had, in addition to the war, is on personnel. These are people with 20, 30 years experience. And then there’s all the impacts you don’t see—the captains and the majors who are looking at what’s happened to those ahead of them and saying, I’m not gonna stick around . That’s years and years of investment that has been lost, and will take years and years and years to replace. Harris: How big of a deal would it be if Defense Secretary Hegseth were impeached? Youssef: Well, it’d be a huge deal. We’ve only had two Cabinet secretaries in the history of the country impeached, neither one of them convicted. Certainly not the person in charge of the largest government organization, the one asking for more than a trillion dollars in government funding, the one responsible for 2 million troops and part of the chain of command. It would be extraordinary, and an incredible condemnation of the top civilian at the Pentagon while the United States has forces deployed and a blockade happening in the Strait of Hormuz. And so it would be an unprecedented thing to happen, in many ways. But by itself, it doesn’t—I don’t think—lead to the sort of foundational questions that need to be asked and answered in terms of: What kind of Defense Department do we want, moving forward? Nichols: It’s a huge deal because Pete Hegseth’s gonna make it a huge deal. A better secretary of defense—and by that I mean almost any secretary of defense—would say, All right, I’m impeached, but we get back to work. You know, life goes on. He would say to the troops: This is not about you . This is something happening in Washington. We’ve got this. But two things will happen, I suspect. One is it will send a message—and I think this is necessary—from the Congress to a lot of people in the high command, the senior command of the United States, that says: Look, we haven’t forgotten that you’re doing things like extrajudicial murders of people in the Caribbean. Just because it’s off the newspapers doesn’t mean that we, the representatives and the people of the United States, have forgotten that you guys were doing this . So that’s a salutary effect, because I think it’s been a tragedy that somehow that just went on and we said, Well, I guess that’s just the way it is . The worst part is that Pete Hegseth will—he’s already done it. He’s going to try to drag the troops into this. These ads where he has himself posing with Stephen Miller and saying, “Stand and fight,” that’s not about the mission of the Defense Department. That’s Pete Hegseth doing an ad for himself that he’s putting out and hoping that the president sees it and doesn’t fire him, but also a message to the troops. It’s us against them. I’m your secretary of defense. These terrible civilian leaders—the ones in the Constitution that, as Nancy points out, that you’re sworn to protect—they’re the enemy now. And so I think it’s necessary. I think it’s important that it happened. But I think that Pete Hegseth will use it to divide the troops even more than he has tried to in the past. And I think that, strangely enough, that’s a good reason to do it. Because that kind of secretary of defense should be impeached and removed. Harris: Well, we’ll have to leave it there. Tom, Nancy, thank you so much for joining me and helping us understand this better and sharing your reporting. Youssef: Thanks for the great conversation. Nichols: Thank you. Harris: That’s all for today’s show. This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Kevin Townsend. It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues at The Atlantic , you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

items.title: Man Utd expected to sack head coach Carrick
items.description: Manchester United look increasingly likely to sack head coach Michael Carrick. The club opted to keep Carrick after the side’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth on 25 October, intending to reassess the situation during this month’s international break. Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that the board remain committed to that process and have not made a final decision on Carrick’s future. However, expectations are growing that chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox will recommend to minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family that they sack Carrick. The 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday means United, who are 18th in the table, have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years. BBC Sport reported in October that the club had sounded out former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann over replacing Carrick. Former Chelsea coach Antonio Conte is keen on the role, while multiple sources told BBC Sport that former Spurs boss Mauricio Pochettino is open to a move to Old Trafford. Pochettino signed a contract extension as USA coach in August. However, the deal is thought to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs. The US have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League play-off with Haiti on 14 and 18 November.

items.description: “Ha sido un debate muy serio. No ha sido exactamente una entrevista”, dijo Santiago Abascal al salir del Teatro Albéniz de Madrid tras grabar su intervención en La revuelta . La que se dio este lunes no fue la típica entrevista televisiva del programa de David Broncano. Tuvo esa incomodidad por la que se ha hecho famoso, sí, pero no por los motivos habituales, sino por la falta de chistes, un público desacostumbrado y un tono de nerviosismo del presentador claramente fuera de su terreno habitual. No hubo tiempo ni para las preguntas clásicas . Ni para Candela . Esto no era La revuelta . Seguir leyendo

items.title: Réseaux sociaux : La HARC lance le recensement des acteurs du secteur
items.description: Lomé, 9 nov. (ATOP)-La Haute Autorité de régulation de la Communication écrite, audiovisuelle et numérique (HARC) invite les créateurs de contenus, blogueurs, influenceurs, TikTokeurs, YouTubeurs et autres acteurs des réseaux sociaux à s’inscrire dans sa base de données, afin de disposer d’informations actualisées sur les intervenants dans cet univers numérique. Dans un communiqué rendu public le 9 novembre à Lomé, le président de la HARC, Pitalounani Telou, demande aux personnes concernées de renseigner un formulaire d’inscription accessible sur le site officiel de l’institution. Les informations sollicitées portent notamment sur les nom et prénoms, le lieu de résidence, le domaine de spécialité ou d’activité sur les réseaux sociaux, ainsi que les coordonnées des intéressés, notamment leur adresse électronique et leur numéro de téléphone. Cette opération vise à permettre à la HARC de constituer une base de données actualisée des acteurs évoluant dans l’univers des réseaux sociaux. Elle devrait également faciliter une meilleure identification des différents intervenants dans cet espace numérique. Au regard de l’importance de cette initiative, le président de la HARC compte sur la mobilisation et la collaboration de l’ensemble des acteurs concernés pour sa réussite. Les personnes intéressées peuvent retrouver les modalités d’inscription sur le site officiel de la HARC : www.harctogo.tg . ATOP/OA/communiqué HARC
